questions.Q8: Q8. What ultimately made you choose your current bank over the alternatives you were considering? What stood out about them?

v.Q8: Simplii won primarily on the fee structure — no monthly fees, full stop. After years of paying fees that felt increasingly unjustifiable, getting to zero was powerfully attractive. And it's backed by CIBC's infrastructure, which meant I felt confident about the deposit security and the backend reliability even if the brand was different. The Interac e-transfer and the mobile deposit capabilities are both solid, and honestly the app is cleaner and easier to use than CIBC's was. It felt like a well-thought-out product rather than a legacy system that had been patched repeatedly. The cash-back savings account was also a nice differentiator.
v.Q5:
So a few things converged. My kids are now adults and financially independent, and I went through a period of really rethinking what I actually need from a bank day-to-day versus what I was paying for. My lifestyle had simplified in some ways — fewer products that I was actively using, but I was still paying the full slate of fees as if I had a complex banking relationship. That started bothering me more than it used to.

The frustration that built up was really about fees relative to value. I was paying somewhere around $30 a month for an account package that I frankly didn't need all the features of, and every time I looked at the statement it irritated me. I also found CIBC's app had gotten clunkier over time — or maybe I'd just gotten used to better interfaces elsewhere. The navigation felt dated and certain things took more taps than they should.

The final straw, honestly, was a fairly minor thing that somehow crystallized everything. I tried to update my contact information through the app and it kept erroring out. I called customer service and was on hold for 41 minutes. Forty-one minutes to update a phone number. When I finally got through, the agent was perfectly pleasant, but by then I'd decided. I'd been meaning to look at alternatives for months and that afternoon I actually did it.
v.Q11: The main frustration is the absence of a branch, which most of the time I don't care about, but occasionally I do. I needed a bank draft recently and had to think creatively about how to get one. And there's no wealth management relationship available through Simplii — I kind of knew that going in, but now that I'm thinking more seriously about retirement in the next ten years or so, I'm finding myself wanting a more integrated advisory conversation that Simplii simply can't offer. Those two things are my biggest gaps.
v.Q10: The no-fee structure has been exactly as advertised — there are no surprises on my monthly statement, which is a genuinely nice feeling. The app has been reliable and the interface is clean. I do most of my banking from my phone and it works. E-transfers are fast. And I think the high-interest savings account rate has been competitive, though I keep most of my savings with EQ Bank anyway. I also appreciate that the customer service wait times, the few times I've needed them, have been much shorter than what I was dealing with at CIBC.

v.Q8: Simplii made sense because it had the full functionality of a checking account with no monthly fee, and the CIBC backbone gave me confidence about security and reliability. The transition was also easier than I expected — linking accounts and getting set up took maybe an hour. And for someone at my life stage, simple and fee-free was genuinely the criteria, and Simplii delivered that clearly.
v.Q5:
I retired about two years ago, and with retirement came a real look at recurring costs. My RBC checking account package was $30 a month. I had kept it because I never really questioned it while I was working, but once I was on a fixed income — investment income and savings draws rather than a salary — that $30 started feeling pointless. I wasn't using half the features in the package.

I also found the app had gotten busier over the years. More promotions, more cross-sell prompts, more clicks to get where I wanted to go. It felt like they were optimizing for selling me things rather than helping me bank.

The decisive moment was fairly simple — I read an article comparing no-fee checking options and realized I was paying $360 a year for essentially the same functionality I could get for free. That was the catalyst.
v.Q11: No branch access is occasionally inconvenient. I needed a certified cheque for a real estate transaction and had to work around it. Customer service wait times have been longer than I'd like on the two occasions I called. And there's no investment or wealth advisory capability, which doesn't matter much today but may matter more in a few years as I think harder about drawdown strategy.
v.Q10: The no-fee promise has held. My monthly statement has no surprises. The app is clean and fast — simpler than RBC's was, which I mean as a compliment. E-transfers work reliably. And honestly the savings account interest rate is competitive. For a retirement lifestyle where my banking is pretty transactional, it fits well.

v.Q8:
Simplii won for a pretty clear set of reasons. First, zero monthly fee — full stop. For the way I actually bank, which is primarily digital with occasional phone support, there's no justification for a monthly account fee. Second, they run on CIBC's infrastructure, which means CIBC ATM access, which means I still have a physical cash option when I need one even though I use it maybe twice a year. That was an important psychological safety net for me.

Third, the high-interest savings account rate was competitive at the time — meaningfully better than RBC's offering. So I could keep my cash working a bit harder without moving it to a separate institution. And fourth — and I know this sounds minor — the onboarding experience was genuinely frictionless. The whole account-opening process took me maybe fifteen minutes online, and I got confirmation immediately. After twelve years of feeling like just another account number at a big bank, there was something refreshing about a setup that didn't require me to come into a branch and sit across from someone trying to upsell me on overdraft protection.
v.Q5:
So the honest trigger was that I paid off my mortgage about two years ago, and that made me sit down and really reassess where all my financial products were and what they were actually costing me. When I took the mortgage out of the equation and looked at what RBC was offering me as a straight chequing-and-savings customer, the value proposition got pretty thin pretty fast.

I was paying around fourteen dollars a month for a chequing account that, when I actually examined my usage, I was primarily using for e-transfers, bill payments, and the occasional deposit. I'm pretty much fully digital — I don't go into branches, I rarely use cash, I don't need a physical footprint. So paying fourteen dollars a month for a network of branches I don't use started to feel like I was subsidizing infrastructure I'd never touch.

The frustration that really crystallized it was a savings rate comparison I did on a whim one afternoon. I had a decent amount sitting in an RBC savings account earning something like 0.01 percent — I am not exaggerating, that was essentially zero. I looked at EQ Bank and they were advertising three-plus percent at the time. I was actually annoyed at myself for not having done this comparison sooner. That gap felt like RBC was just banking on my inertia.

And then there was a customer service interaction where I called to ask about upgrading to a higher-tier account to potentially get better rates, and the person I spoke to was kind of dismissive — like they weren't very motivated to help me optimize my relationship. That was the final piece. I had been with them for twelve years and it felt like that tenure meant nothing to them. Within a week I was researching alternatives seriously.
v.Q11: I think the honest frustration is that the product breadth is limited. I can't get a mortgage through Simplii — well, technically through CIBC but not a Simplii-native product — and there's no investment account option within the Simplii interface itself. I've ended up building a bit of a multi-institution setup as a result, which means I'm managing accounts in a few different places. That's fine, and maybe that's just the modern banking reality, but occasionally I wish there were a single interface that brought everything together. There's also no physical branch option if I genuinely needed that, which I've known from the start but still notice occasionally as a gap. And I'd say the credit card product isn't as strong as what some dedicated credit card providers offer — the rewards aren't particularly competitive if you're optimizing for that.
v.Q10: The no-fee structure continues to be the thing I appreciate most. It is genuinely liberating to not think about a banking fee line item every month. The app has improved since I first joined — it's cleaner now, it covers everything I actually need on a daily basis, and I've had no issues with transfers or payments. E-transfer has been seamless. And I think the savings rates, while they fluctuate with the rate environment, have generally stayed competitive compared to what I'd get if I went back to a big bank. I've also had two interactions with customer service over the twenty months — one about a payment timing question and one about account settings — and both were resolved without major frustration, which met my expectations.

v.Q8: Simplii won primarily on the fee elimination — the idea of paying zero per month for my checking when I do everything digitally anyway just made immediate sense to me. But I also found their app cleaner and more intuitive than I expected given that I hadn't really looked at them carefully before. And the CIBC connection — they share ATMs and they're genuinely a CIBC subsidiary — meant I was keeping some continuity of the ATM network without paying CIBC's fees. That felt like a smart compromise. The switch itself was also remarkably low friction, which I appreciated.
v.Q5: So the big life context was that my mortgage came up for renewal. That became the moment where I actually sat down and evaluated everything, because I was going to be shopping the mortgage anyway. And when I looked at my checking account with fresh eyes during that process, I realized I had been paying a monthly fee that was hard to justify — I'm someone who does basically everything online and I was paying for branch access I almost never used. The frustration had been simmering for a while, actually. I'd had two instances in the previous year where I needed help and called CIBC, and both times the hold time was excessive — I'm talking twenty-five, thirty minutes — and when I got through, the representatives seemed constrained in what they could actually resolve. I didn't feel like a seventeen-year customer, I felt like a number in a queue. And then the mortgage renewal quote from CIBC was not competitive. I got a significantly better rate elsewhere, and that was kind of the moment I thought, well, if I'm leaving for the mortgage, why am I keeping them for checking? I decided to make a clean break.
v.Q11: The thing I notice most is the absence of in-person support. If I had a truly complex financial situation to talk through, I'd want to sit across from someone, and Simplii doesn't offer that. I've also found their credit card product lineup pretty thin — there aren't many options and the rewards aren't compelling compared to what's out there. And occasionally their app feels like it's the junior version of a larger platform, which I guess it kind of is given the CIBC connection. Nothing severe, but those are the gaps.
v.Q10: The zero fee structure genuinely delivers what it promised — I've had no surprise charges in nineteen months, which sounds basic but is actually meaningful to me given my history. The app is clean and fast. E-transfers go through quickly. And the customer service, when I've needed it — twice in nineteen months — has been notably better than what I was experiencing at CIBC in terms of wait times. Not dramatically warmer, but much more efficient. I also appreciate the savings rate on their high-interest account, which is competitive.

v.Q8: So Simplii won for a combination of reasons that all pointed in the same direction. The most concrete one was the zero monthly fee with direct deposit — I do direct deposit, I always will, so that condition was trivially met, and the idea of paying literally nothing for my primary checking account when I was paying twelve to fifteen dollars a month at RBC was compelling in a very simple, legible way. But it wasn't only that. The CIBC ATM access was genuinely important to me — I was a little worried about going to a bank with no branches, and knowing I could use CIBC ATMs for free took away that anxiety. The onboarding was also notably quick and clear, which created a positive first impression. And I guess I'd say my friend's experience gave me social proof that mattered — I wasn't jumping into something unknown, I was following someone whose judgment I trusted into something that had worked for them. That combination of price logic, infrastructure access, and peer validation made it feel like the right call.
v.Q5:
So the timing of the switch was connected to two things happening at once. First, I got a new job with a salary bump, and for the first time I was really sitting down and thinking about my finances more carefully — like, actually optimizing rather than just letting things run on autopilot. That made me scrutinize every recurring cost, including my banking fees. And the second thing was that I'd just helped a close friend move and he had switched to Simplii months earlier and kept telling me how the zero-fee structure was straightforwardly better for people in our situation — we're renters, we do everything digitally, we don't need tellers. That planted a real seed.

But there were frustrations too, and I should be honest about those. The monthly fee at RBC — I was on a plan that technically could be waived but I kept dipping in and out of the qualifying conditions, and some months I'd just get charged the fee without really noticing because the threshold requirements were opaque. It wasn't massive money but it added up and it felt like the bank was quietly benefiting from my inattention, which bothered me more than the dollar amount. I also had a specific incident that I keep coming back to — I had a fraud alert on my card, legitimate thing, RBC caught it and froze the card, which is fine and correct. But then the process to get it unfrozen was genuinely painful. I had to call, wait on hold for about twenty-two minutes, get transferred, explain the whole thing again, get transferred again, and it took nearly an hour for what felt like it should be a ten-minute resolution. And at the end of that call I thought, this is a bank I've been loyal to for nine years and this is what the experience is when I actually need help. That was kind of the moment the relationship started feeling transactional rather than reciprocal. A few weeks later I started actually researching alternatives instead of just thinking about it.
v.Q11: I'd say there are a few things, none of them severe enough to send me looking, but real. The credit card I got through Simplii is fine but the rewards are pretty underwhelming — I ended up keeping my old RBC Avion card specifically because I couldn't find a Simplii card that competed on travel points. That's a wallet fragmentation I didn't want but accepted. The app also has some rough edges — the transaction search is not great, and the bill payment interface feels a bit dated compared to what I've seen at other banks. And there's a certain intangible thing where I do sometimes miss having a physical place I could walk into with something complicated. Not enough to act on, but I've had moments where I wanted to sit across from a person.
v.Q10: So the zero fee has just quietly delivered in the background for twenty months and that's exactly what I wanted — I don't think about banking costs because there aren't really any. The app does the core things I need cleanly and quickly: I can send e-transfers, check my balance, see my transactions categorized, and pay bills without any real friction. I also think the savings account interest rate is competitive — I have a bit parked there while I figure out my longer-term investment plan, and I'm getting more than I would at RBC. Customer service has been faster than I expected for a digital bank — the one time I had a question I got through on the phone in a reasonable amount of time and the person was helpful. And I think honestly the mental relief of not having a complicated fee structure with conditions I need to track is something I undervalued before I experienced the alternative.

v.Q8: Honestly, Simplii won the comparison pretty cleanly once I laid it out. No monthly fee with direct deposit, which solved the specific problem I was trying to fix. The CIBC ATM network access took away my worry about being stuck without cash withdrawal options. And when I actually tested the app through their demo materials, it was clean and covered everything I do day-to-day. The signup process was also genuinely fast — I think I had an account open within a day, which removed any excuse to procrastinate. It felt like the decision with the fewest downsides.
v.Q5: So the trigger was pretty mundane, honestly — I was doing a personal budget review at the start of the year and I just lined up all my monthly recurring expenses. And there it was: a $16.95 monthly fee for my BMO checking account, every single month. When I actually looked at what I was getting for that, I couldn't really justify it. I had direct deposit and I was meeting the balance threshold maybe seven or eight months out of twelve, so I was actually paying the fee more months than not. That bothered me once I made it visible — it had just been a line item I ignored. On top of that, I'd had a frustrating experience trying to dispute what I thought was a duplicate charge on a bill payment. I called BMO, the hold time was long, and when I got through, the person I spoke to was polite but the resolution took over a week of back-and-forth. I kept having to follow up. That combination of quiet monthly costs and a service experience that wasn't responsive — I started asking myself why I was staying. And once I started asking that question, the answer was basically just inertia.
v.Q11: A couple of things come to mind. The credit card options are pretty thin — I kept my BMO cash back card because I couldn't find a Simplii card that matched it for that reward type, so I've ended up with more cards than I wanted. And I do notice the absence of a physical branch in moments where I have a slightly more complicated question — I once tried to get clarity on some account settings and the chat support was helpful but slower than I'd like. It's not a dealbreaker, but there's a ceiling on how complex an issue I'd want to handle purely through digital channels.
v.Q10: The no-fee structure has just worked exactly as advertised, which is kind of all I wanted. I don't think about checking account fees anymore and that's genuinely nice. The app is clean and stable — I haven't had any of the reliability issues I was somewhat worried about going to a digital-only bank. And I've found their savings account interest rate to be meaningfully better than what I had at BMO, so I've parked some of my short-term savings there too. The e-transfer experience is quick and intuitive. Nothing flashy, but it does the job well.

v.Q8: Simplii stood out for a few reasons. No monthly fee was the headline, obviously, but the thing that actually convinced me was that they're backed by CIBC — and I know that sounds paradoxical given that I left CIBC, but it meant I trusted the infrastructure. The deposits are CDIC-protected, and there's interoperability with CIBC ATMs which meant I'd have physical cash access without fees. The digital experience looked clean and straightforward when I previewed it. And honestly, a neighbour of mine had been using Simplii for about three years and was very positive about the reliability and the customer service. When you're my age and you've had the same bank for twenty years, that kind of personal reference carries a lot of weight.
v.Q5: So the context — my business had a difficult stretch during 2021 and 2022, and I was looking hard at every cost. One of the things I looked at was what I was paying in personal banking fees. I had a premium personal account at CIBC that was costing me about $30 a month, and when I actually sat down and looked at what I was getting for that, it didn't add up anymore. I wasn't using the bundled services that justified the fee. So I called CIBC to ask about moving to a lower-fee option or getting a fee waiver, and the conversation was frankly disappointing. The person I spoke to was polite but essentially said that based on my account balances I didn't qualify for a waiver, and offered me a downgrade that would have removed features I did use. It felt like a dead end. That was the frustration that got me looking. And then when I started looking at alternatives, I realized how much the digital banking landscape had changed. I had stayed with CIBC partly out of habit and familiarity, and I guess I hadn't really kept up with what else was available. Once I started actually comparing, the fee differential was stark — I was used to paying fees as just a cost of banking, and the idea that I could get solid personal banking with no monthly fee at all was genuinely surprising to me. v.Q11: The product range is narrower than I was used to, and that's a real limitation for someone at my stage. They don't have a full wealth management or investment advisory service, so if I ever wanted to consolidate my investments there, I couldn't. And they don't have business banking, which means I'm still maintaining my business accounts elsewhere — that two-bank setup adds some administrative overhead. I'd also say the savings interest rate, while better than the big banks, is still not as competitive as EQ Bank, so I sometimes wonder if I should have a third account just for savings. v.Q10: The no-fee structure has been exactly what it promised, no surprises. The digital experience is clean and functional — I can do everything I need from my phone, which suits me fine. And accessing cash through CIBC ATMs has been seamless, so I don't feel like I've lost anything on that front. Their phone customer service has been responsive when I've needed it — once I called about an unusual transaction and was connected to someone within a few minutes who resolved it on the call. I also appreciate that they don't constantly try to cross-sell me every time I log in. The interface is purposeful rather than noisy.

v.Q8: Simplii won on the no-fee promise and the CIBC infrastructure backing it. I want no monthly fee, but I also need to trust that the institution is stable and the deposits are protected, and Simplii gave me both of those things. The access to CIBC ATMs across Canada was a practical consideration — I didn't want to be hunting for surcharge-free ATMs. And the onboarding process was genuinely smooth. I set everything up online in under half an hour, which after the bureaucratic experience I'd had with RBC during the account change process felt like a revelation. The interest rate on the savings account, while not at EQ Bank levels, was meaningfully better than RBC. And I read a lot of reviews from people who had used Simplii for several years and the recurring theme was reliability without surprises, which is honestly what I wanted after a disruptive period in my personal life.
v.Q5: So the life context — I had separated from my spouse about two and a half years ago, and going through that process meant untangling a lot of joint financial accounts. In doing that, I essentially had to rebuild my personal banking from scratch, and that created a natural moment to ask whether I should just rebuild it at RBC or whether I should take the opportunity to move. And when I looked at the numbers with fresh eyes, the fees were the first thing that jumped out. I had been on a premium account paying $30 a month, and when I calculated what that added up to over fifteen years it was a genuinely uncomfortable number for what I was actually receiving. I also, during the separation process, had a frustrating experience with RBC's support when I needed to update account access and notification settings. I was on hold for a long time, and when I finally reached someone the process was surprisingly bureaucratic for what felt like it should be a straightforward request. There was also a savings rate issue — I had a meaningful amount sitting in an RBC savings account earning essentially nothing, and I knew by that point that I could do significantly better elsewhere. So it was the combination of the fee rethink, the service frustration during a vulnerable time, and the low savings return all converging at the same moment when I was already making changes anyway. It wasn't dramatic but it was clear.
v.Q11: Honestly, the product depth is my main frustration. I've moved on from the phase of my life where I want everything at one bank, but Simplii can't hold my mortgage, doesn't have a proper investment advisory service, and doesn't offer the kind of structured financial planning I'm starting to think about as I get into my mid-forties. So by necessity I'm spread across multiple institutions. That's manageable but it's not ideal. I'd also say the savings rate, while better than RBC, is still below what EQ Bank offers, so I do keep a separate account there for larger cash reserves. And there's no in-person option if I ever needed one for something complex.
v.Q10: The no-fee structure is exactly as advertised — I have not paid a monthly fee since I switched, which sounds simple but after years of paying for banking it is genuinely satisfying. The digital experience is clean and I can do everything I need without any friction. Their e-transfer setup is fast and the limits are reasonable. And when I had a question about a hold on a large deposit — a legitimate one from a property sale — I called and reached someone relatively quickly who explained the hold period clearly. The transparency of that interaction stood out to me. I also like that I don't feel like I'm being marketed to constantly when I log in.

v.Q8:
Simplii won for me on a pretty clear combination of factors. The zero monthly fee was the most obvious one — I was basically going from paying over two hundred dollars a year in account fees to paying nothing, and I couldn't identify a meaningful difference in the day-to-day functionality that would justify that cost. That's a very clean value proposition.

But I think what actually pushed me over the line beyond the fee thing was the CIBC ATM access. Because Simplii is backed by CIBC, you get access to the full CIBC ATM network at no charge, and there are CIBC machines all over Edmonton. So I wasn't giving up physical cash access, which was one of my concerns about going fully digital. That felt like a real differentiator versus Tangerine, where your ATM story is more complicated.

And then my colleague's years of positive experience was genuinely influential. He's someone I trust, he's financially thoughtful, and he'd been with them for a long time without complaints. That social proof mattered, probably more than I expected it to going into the decision.
v.Q5:
So the trigger, if I'm being honest, was a combination of things that had been building for a while and then one specific incident that just made me say, okay, enough.

On the life side, my partner and I had just refinanced our mortgage — we went with a different lender for the renewal because TD's rate at the time was not competitive, and that whole process made me start thinking more critically about whether TD was actually the best place for each piece of my financial life. So refinancing the mortgage with someone else was the first crack.

But the frustrations had been accumulating for a couple of years before that. The fees were a constant irritant. I was paying a monthly fee on my chequing account — I think it was around sixteen or seventeen dollars a month — and every time I'd look at my statement and see that line item, I'd think, what am I actually getting for this? Because the features weren't noticeably better than what I knew some of the no-fee digital banks were offering. My colleague at work had been using Simplii for years and kept telling me he wasn't paying a cent in monthly fees and had access to all the same basic functionality. That planted a seed.

And then there was the customer service piece. I had a situation — this was the final straw, honestly — where I had a fraud alert on my account because of a purchase I'd made while travelling. Legitimate purchase, my card flagged it anyway, which I understand can happen. But the process to resolve it was absolutely maddening. I spent forty-five minutes on hold, got transferred twice, had to re-explain the situation from scratch each time because there was clearly no continuity between agents. By the end of it I had resolved the issue, but I felt so genuinely disrespected by the process. Like, I have been a customer for eighteen years, I've held multiple products with you, and this is how you handle my time? That was the moment I actually sat down and started properly researching alternatives.
v.Q11:

The first one is that there's no physical branch — I knew this going in, and ninety-nine percent of the time it doesn't matter at all, but there have been two occasions where I wanted to do something that felt like it warranted a face-to-face conversation, and I just couldn't. One was a question about a larger wire transfer I was considering, and I ended up calling, which was fine, but in the back of my mind I thought, it would be nice to just go sit down with someone.

v.Q10:

The CIBC ATM network matters because I do occasionally need cash, and I didn't want to be hunting for a surcharge-free machine. v.Q8: The no-monthly-fee was the core thing — it was the whole reason I started looking and Simplii delivered it cleanly. But beyond that, the fact that they're backed by CIBC gave me comfort. I'm not putting my money with some fintech startup I've never heard of. There's real infrastructure behind it. The e-Transfer experience is seamless, I can deposit cheques through the app, and there's no limit on transactions that would force me into a fee situation. The signup process was also really smooth — entirely online, took maybe twenty minutes, and I was set up within a couple of days. That ease-of-entry mattered because I'd been dreading the admin of switching and it turned out to be much less painful than I expected.
v.Q5:
So the life context was that my partner and I bought our first home about eighteen months ago, and going through that whole process — the mortgage, the legal costs, all of it — made me genuinely look at every line item in our budget. For the first time I was sitting down and saying, okay, what is this monthly bank fee actually getting me?

I was paying around $16.95 a month at Scotia for a plan that I genuinely could not justify anymore. I was doing basically everything digitally. I hadn't set foot in a branch in probably eight months. And when I started comparing, I realized I could get a no-fee chequing account at Simplii that did everything I actually needed.

The frustration that kind of pushed me over the edge was a customer service call where I asked about reducing my monthly fee — I'd seen that they had some promotional offers — and the person I spoke to was just totally unhelpful. They went through a script, offered me a temporary $3 discount, and basically made me feel like I was asking for too much. After buying a house I was a bit sensitive to costs, so that conversation stuck with me. Within two weeks I had opened a Simplii account and started moving things over.
v.Q11: Honestly the biggest one is that there's no physical branch I can walk into if something gets complicated. So far nothing has required that, but it's a kind of background anxiety. The other thing is that the savings rate outside of promotional periods is kind of average — not bad, but not best-in-class either. And I sometimes find the website a bit confusing when I'm trying to find account details or old statements on desktop. The app is better than the website, which feels a bit backwards. Nothing that's made me want to leave, but those are the friction points.
v.Q10: The no-fee experience has been exactly what I wanted — there are genuinely no surprise charges showing up. The app is clean and straightforward. I think their high-interest savings account promos have been a nice bonus — they run these promotional rates pretty regularly and I've taken advantage of a couple of them. Customer service, I've only needed to call once and it was fine, reasonably quick. And I like that because it's tied to CIBC's network, I can use CIBC ATMs without fees, which covers me pretty well geographically.

v.Q8: The no-fee structure was the primary driver, full stop. But what distinguished Simplii from Tangerine, which also has no fees, was the combination of the CIBC ATM access and the fact that the app seemed cleaner and more modern when I compared them side by side. I also valued the ability to use CIBC ATMs for free, because even though I said I'm mostly digital, there are moments when you need cash and paying $3 every time at a random ATM is annoying. Having a real ATM network backstop felt like the best of both worlds — no fee, no branches, but not stranded without cash access either.
v.Q5:
So the context was that my partner and I started getting serious about buying a place — we'd been renting in Calgary and were thinking about a condo or a townhouse. That process made me look much more carefully at my overall financial setup than I ever had before, and honestly the first thing that jumped out was the fees I was paying TD every month.

I was on a plan that cost me $16.95 a month, and when I really broke down what I was getting for that, it was essentially just unlimited transactions. I'm not a heavy branch user, I do basically everything online, and it dawned on me that I was paying over $200 a year for infrastructure I was barely using. That had been true for years but I'd never stopped to actually calculate it.

Beyond the fees, I had some frustrating interactions with TD's customer service around the mortgage pre-approval process. There was a lot of back-and-forth, documents I had to resubmit, and communication that felt fragmented — one person would tell me one thing and then I'd get a different answer from someone else. That lack of coordination was maddening when you're already stressed about a big financial decision.

The final push was a Reddit thread, honestly. I know that sounds ridiculous but I came across a pretty detailed thread comparing no-fee banks and Simplii kept coming up positively, and someone had laid out the math on what you save over five years by eliminating the monthly fee. It clicked. I opened the Simplii account the next weekend and did the full switch over about three weeks.
v.Q11:
Customer service is the weak point. I had one issue about eight months in — a payment had posted to the wrong account and I needed to sort it out — and getting a human being on the phone took way longer than it should have. The chat function wasn't helpful for something that nuanced. I eventually got it resolved but it took three contacts over two days, which felt disproportionate to the problem.

I also find the savings rate on the basic savings account underwhelming — I know that's kind of the trade-off for no monthly fee, but it does mean I keep my savings elsewhere. And the app, while fine, lacks some of the more advanced budgeting or spending-insights features that I've seen in some newer fintech tools. It's functional but not particularly sophisticated.
v.Q10: The no-fee thing delivers exactly what it promised — I've genuinely not paid a monthly banking fee in 16 months and that still feels like a small win every time I think about it. The app is functional and clean, e-transfers are fast, and the CIBC ATM access has worked exactly as advertised. I've also found that for straightforward transactions, the experience is smooth and basically frictionless. It does what I need a checking account to do without adding cost or complexity.

v.Q8: The CIBC ATM network access was honestly a big factor. I know it sounds ironic given that I left CIBC, but keeping access to their ATMs without paying for their accounts felt like a smart move. No monthly fee plus real ATM access was the combination I wanted. And since it's backed by CIBC, I figured the operational reliability wouldn't be a concern. It felt like a low-risk switch.
v.Q5:
So I got a salary increase at work and moved apartments at the same time, and when I moved I kind of used it as a chance to audit all my monthly expenses. The no-fee status on my CIBC account had lapsed — I was now paying $14.95 a month — and I hadn't really noticed because I wasn't tracking it carefully.

Once I noticed, it annoyed me. I did some quick research and realized Simplii was basically the same infrastructure — it's backed by CIBC, same ATM network — but no monthly fee. That felt like a pretty obvious switch.

There wasn't a dramatic incident or a big frustration beyond the fees, honestly. CIBC had just become the default option rather than the considered choice, and once I looked at it critically the value wasn't there for me anymore.
v.Q11: The savings rate is pretty low — I keep a small buffer there but I'd never park real savings in it given what other places offer. And I find the app a little limited for anything beyond the basics — there's no real spending categorization or budget view, which I've come to expect from banking apps at this point. It also just feels a bit bare-bones visually. None of that is a dealbreaker, but I'd say the product has stayed pretty static in the time I've been using it.
v.Q10: It does the basics well without charging me for it, which is really all I wanted. The app is functional, e-transfers go through quickly, and the ATM access has worked perfectly. I genuinely cannot complain about the core product. For someone who doesn't need in-person banking regularly, it hits the mark.

v.Q8: No monthly fee, it's backed by CIBC so I felt comfortable about stability, and the e-transfer and bill pay functionality was basically identical to what I had at BMO. The savings account interest rate was also pretty competitive at the time I switched. It really came down to getting the same thing for free instead of paying almost $17 a month.
v.Q5: I was paying $16.95 a month for an account and I started questioning what I was actually getting for that. I did some research and found Simplii offered essentially the same functionality with no monthly fee. There wasn't a dramatic incident — I just kind of woke up and did the math. I think I'd been vaguely annoyed about the fees for a while but hadn't acted on it. The final push was honestly reading a personal finance subreddit thread where someone laid out the comparison really clearly. I thought, this is ridiculous, why am I paying this.
v.Q11: The main frustration is that there's no physical branch, so for anything that needs an in-person conversation I have to go to a CIBC branch and explain the Simplii relationship, which is a bit awkward. Phone wait times can be long when I've needed to call. And they don't offer a full investment product suite, so I've had to keep those products elsewhere anyway.
v.Q10: I like that it does what I need without charging me for it. The app is clean and straightforward. E-transfers go through quickly. I haven't had any problems that required me to contact support, which is probably the best thing I can say. It's simple and it works.
